preamble: Diphthongization of stressed [a] to [ie] after a palatal or palatalized consonant is Bartsch's law, a 5th–6th century change of northern Gallo-Romance: Latin a in stressed open syllables preceded by a palatal or palatalized consonant became Old French ie, as in cārum > chier, laxāre > laissier and canem > chien. Whether the path ran through an intermediate [aɛ] diphthong or a raised [e] is unresolved, but the attested Old French outcome is [ie]. Outside this law a direct a > ie shift is rare; the Spanish ie of piedra and tierra comes from Latin short e, not a.

examples.note: Stressed open-syllable a after the palatalized velar (Latin k > tʃ before a) became ie by Bartsch's law; modern French cher [ʃɛʁ] later reduced the diphthong.
Modern French laisser; the ie was later reduced after the palatal.
Same conditioning; the ie diphthong survives in modern French chien [ʃjɛ̃].
Source of English chief; modern French chef.
